newsitem.title: INDIA: India ready to send envoy to Pakistan if invited.
newsitem.headline: India ready to send envoy to Pakistan if invited.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda was quoted on Thursday as saying he would send Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral to Pakistan for talks if Islamabad extended an invitation.

"As soon as I receive the invitation, I will ask the external affairs minister to go to Pakistan for talks," the Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Deve Gowda as telling troops in Kashmir. "We want to improve our relations with Islamabad."
"We are ready to respond constructively," said Deve Gowda, who was visiting soldiers near the line of control dividing Jammu and Kashmir state from the one third of Kashmir ruled by Pakistan.
The Indian leader recalled Pakistani prime minister-elect Nawaz Sharif's recent statement offering dialogue to usher in a new era in relations between the longtime foes.
"Mr Sharif's initial views have been favourable and I hope that the new government in Pakistan will show a positive approach in this regard," the news agency quoted Deve Gowda as saying.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947, two of them over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.

Deve Gowda and ousted Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto exchanged letters after the Indian prime minister took office last June, but the notes did not lead to high-level bilateral talks, which were last held in January 1994.
Sharif's overwhelming victory in Pakistan's general elections earlier this month has raised hopes that peace talks could be resumed.
The bilateral talks which broke down three years ago were led by the two countries' foreign secretaries, who are the highest ranking civil servants in the foreign ministries.
Analysts said Deve Gowda's willingness to dispatch his foreign minister to Pakistan appeared to underscore his seriousness in reopening a dialogue with Islamabad.
Pakistan has long insisted two sides resolve their differences over Kashmir before taking up other bilateral issues.

But New Delhi has rejected Islamabad's insistence that an internationally supervised plebiscite be held in Kashmir to determine the region's future status. Delhi considers Jammu and Kashmir to be an integral part of India and rejects outside involvement in the dispute.

India accuses Pakistan of arming and training militants fighting New Delhi's rule in Jammu and Kashmir, where more than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since a separatist rebellion erupted in 1990.
Islamabad says it provides the guerrillas only diplomatic and moral support.
